title: When the Winter Breaks
premise: When Jonah Ravensworth's twin sister Wren dies, the family buries the body under Wren's name — but Jonah knows it isn't Wren in the coffin, because Jonah is the one who came home and found their sister already gone, replaced by something that smiles with her face. The house they inherited reflects rooms a second behind, and in that stolen second Jonah glimpses 1974: the year their grandmother took a life to save her children and buried the debt in the mirrors. To free Wren's soul from the glass, Jonah must uncover the grandmother's crime, return what was stolen — the life of a boy the town forgot — and decide whether love for a twin justifies repeating the original sin. In the end Jonah shatters every mirror and gives the house their own reflection in trade, walking out half-remembered while Wren, restored, carries the truth no one will believe.
about_author: Sable Okafor is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing estate sales in rural New England, where she learned that every old house keeps at least one ledger it never meant to show. She writes horror about inheritance, guilt, and the documents families leave behind like wounds.

chapters.title: The Wrong Body
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Jonah arrives home for Wren's funeral and realizes at the open casket that the body is not their twin — the hands are wrong, the scar missing. Grief curdles into dread as the family, oddly calm, urges them not to look too closely. Beat: the ground opens beneath certainty.

chapters.title: A Ledger of Small Doubts
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Unable to sleep, Jonah begins documenting everything — photographs, timestamps, notes — a habit inherited from their grandmother's meticulous journals. The entries start contradicting each other; a clock in the hall runs one second slow. Beat: documentation as prayer, prayer beginning to fail.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Jonah notices the hallway mirror shows the room a beat late — and in that lag, a figure standing where no one stands. They test it with a metronome and a camera. The camera captures nothing; the mirror is patient. Beat: the house admits it is haunted, politely.

chapters.title: Wren's Room, Unchanged
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Jonah searches their twin's room and finds it preserved like a museum, dust undisturbed for weeks — yet Wren supposedly died three days ago. A hairbrush still holds warm water. Beat: the funeral was theater, and someone in the family is performing.

chapters.title: The Aunt Who Smiles Too Slowly
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Aunt Corinne, executor of the estate, deflects every question about the body and the mirrors with rehearsed warmth. At dinner she answers a question a half-second before Jonah asks it. Beat: loyalty in the family is revealed as complicity.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Journals, 1974
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. In the attic, Jonah finds their grandmother's ledgers — immaculate records ending abruptly in October 1974 with a single line: 'The glass keeps what we cannot pay.' A page has been torn out. Beat: the past has a paper trail, and it leads downward.

chapters.title: The Boy in the Photograph
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Among the journals, a photo of two children: Wren's age, and a boy no family member will name. In town, the historical society has no record of him — his file razored out in 1974. Beat: justice outside the law begins with restoring a name.

chapters.title: Reflection, Interrupted
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Inside the mirror, Wren exists in a frozen amber second, aware but unable to move, watching Jonah through the glass like weather. She learns the mirror-world's rules: it trades, it keeps, it waits. Beat: love against duty from the trapped side.

chapters.title: The House Remembers Water
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. A flooded basement, drained decades ago, still echoes with splashing at night. Jonah finds the torn journal page waterlogged but legible: their grandmother drowned a boy to save Wren's mother from his father's violence — and paid the mirrors to keep the secret. Beat: the sin was love, once.

chapters.title: Corinne's Confession
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Confronted with the page, Aunt Corinne admits the family has fed the mirrors a Ravensworth every generation to keep the debt deferred. Wren was this generation's payment; the body in the casket was a bought substitute. Beat: duty dressed as protection, exposed as sacrifice.

chapters.title: What the Glass Wants
chapters.summary: POV Wren. The mirror offers Wren a bargain: stay willingly and the house will spare Jonah forever. She nearly accepts, hearing Jonah's footsteps overhead like a heartbeat. Beat: the temptation of self-erasure in the name of love.

chapters.title: The Town That Forgot
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Jonah tracks the drowned boy's surviving sister, now elderly, who has spent fifty years writing letters no one answers. She gives Jonah the boy's name — Elias — and his only possession, a tin whistle. Beat: truth as an obligation that outlives everyone.

chapters.title: Nine Mirrors, Nine Debts
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Jonah maps the house's mirrors and finds nine, each older, each lagging a different interval — a ledger of payments. The oldest mirror shows 1974 continuously, the night playing on loop. Beat: the architecture of the debt made visible.

chapters.title: The Second That Opens
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. At 3:33 a.m., the lag widens and Jonah is pulled through the hall mirror into the amber second, where the house's past is layered like sediment. They see Elias, drowned, still waiting at the edge of the water for someone to say his name. Beat: horror becomes pilgrimage.

chapters.title: Reunion in Amber
chapters.summary: POV both. Jonah and Wren find each other inside the lag, able to speak for the first time since the funeral. Wren reveals the mirrors' price: a life for a life, returned or replaced. Beat: joy inside a trap, sharpening the stakes.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. The house, speaking through Corinne's smiling reflection, offers Jonah the old deal: give a life, take Wren home, keep the secret. It shows them Elias's sister's face and promises she'll finally rest too. Beat: the system offers to make Jonah complicit.

chapters.title: Corinne Pays
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Refusing, Jonah triggers the debt's acceleration; the house begins collecting from Corinne, aging her by decades in hours as she once aged the mirrors' patience. She dies asking forgiveness, and the mirrors grant it by keeping her reflection. Beat: the cost of complicity, collected.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Jonah performs the counter-rite from the journals: naming Elias, giving his whistle and his sister's letters to the water in the basement, formally returning the stolen life. The mirrors begin to crack from the oldest outward. Beat: justice outside the law, enacted as ceremony.

chapters.title: The House Fights Back
chapters.summary: POV Wren. The mirrors, dying, flood the house with every deferred second at once — fifty years of drowned night. Wren holds the passage open from inside while Jonah drags Elias's name into the light. Beat: climax, loyalty tested at the point of breaking.

chapters.title: A Life for a Life
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. The final mirror demands payment before it breaks. Jonah offers their own reflection — their memory, their face, their place in photographs — and the house accepts. Beat: the price of doing right is being forgotten by the record.

chapters.title: The Winter Breaks
chapters.summary: POV Jonah, dimly. Jonah wakes on the porch in thawing March, Wren alive beside them, Elias's whistle silent at last. But Jonah's face is absent from every photograph, every mirror, every memory but Wren's. Beat: bittersweet dawn, the debt paid in identity.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Wren, restored, begins her own ledger — writing Jonah into existence page by page, testimony against a world that no longer remembers them. The house stands empty, its mirrors all shattered but one, which reflects only now, on time. Beat: love against duty, continued as authorship.
